title: Types of economic systems and economic resources — 1.2.1

blocks.heading: Land: the natural contribution
blocks.text: In economics, land comprises natural resources used in production. It includes more than the ground occupied by a building. Water, fish stocks, mineral deposits, forest resources and the productive qualities of a site can all contribute. In an original crop-growing example, the soil and water are land, whereas an installed pump is capital. The distinction is about origin and function: the pump is a produced asset that helps use the natural resource. The payment for using land is conventionally called rent. Do not infer that every natural resource can be obtained without a cost because nature originally supplied it. Access, extraction and competing uses can make it scarce and valuable. A business choosing one site over another compares qualities such as access to water, soil suitability and distance from its customers.

blocks.heading: Using natural resources responsibly
blocks.text: A shoreline can support fishing, tourism and conservation interests. Allocating it to one use may restrict another. The quantity of a natural resource is not the same as the amount that can be used sustainably each year. Better knowledge or equipment can make some resources easier to use, while depletion or damage can reduce what remains available. A campsite may benefit from scenery without owning the surrounding mountains. Its activity still depends on a natural contribution. When identifying land in a case, point to the natural resource rather than naming the business's cash account. Keep an improvement such as a constructed access road separate from the underlying site. These distinctions become useful when analysing how an activity combines natural resources with equipment and human effort, and when comparing current use with future availability.

blocks.heading: Labour: physical and mental effort
blocks.text: Labour is human physical and mental effort used in production. A mechanic diagnosing a fault, an office worker organising orders and a farm worker harvesting crops all supply labour. The contribution is not limited to manual work. Wages and salaries reward employed labour, while the terms of employment and the nature of the task can vary. Distinguish the quantity of labour available from its quality. The number of people and their working hours affect quantity. Skills, experience, education and health can affect how effectively that time is used. A trained worker may diagnose a fault more accurately, reducing the time and materials needed for reworking. This does not mean a change in training instantly improves every task; relevance, practice and the equipment available also matter.

blocks.heading: Labour quality and labour availability
blocks.text: Suppose a furniture workshop has four employees, each available for the same hours as last month. A relevant training programme may improve their ability to read plans without increasing the number of workers. This is a possible change in labour quality, rather than an automatic increase in the labour force. Conversely, extending opening hours may increase the labour time needed without making the employees more skilled. The two changes require different explanations. Health problems, absence or a mismatch between skills and tasks can restrict effective labour even when the headcount is unchanged. When a case describes a salaried supervisor directing staff, that person's mental effort is labour. Look for responsibility for organising and risking the venture before identifying a separate entrepreneurial contribution. Topic 4.2 develops the rewards and differences in earnings associated with labour.

blocks.heading: Capital: produced means of production
blocks.text:
Capital means produced resources used to make other goods and services. Tools, machinery, delivery equipment and productive buildings are examples. A tailoring business can use sewing machines and a cutting table to make clothing; these assets provide productive services rather than being goods purchased for direct personal satisfaction. The same physical object can have a different economic role in another setting. A vehicle used to carry business deliveries is capital for that activity, while a household's vehicle used for personal journeys is a consumer durable. Explain the use in the case instead of classifying an item by its appearance alone. More capital equipment can help workers produce, but its usefulness depends on suitability, maintenance, skills and demand for the output. Buying an unsuitable machine can tie up resources without creating the expected gain.

The reward for capital is interest.

blocks.heading: Capital goods and financial resources
blocks.text: Money can finance a purchase of capital equipment, but money is not the productive machine itself. In this productive sense, investment adds to the stock of capital goods. A mill purchasing an additional grain grinder makes productive investment. Moving existing money from one account to another is a financial transaction and does not by itself add a grinder. Financial arrangements can support later investment, so the distinction does not imply that banking is unimportant. It identifies which step has actually occurred. Capital goods can wear out or become outdated, meaning some investment replaces existing assets rather than increasing the net stock. When explaining an example, state whether the business is financing equipment, acquiring equipment or using equipment to produce output. Topic 2.3 explains financial institutions, while topic 5.2 explains how the combination of equipment and labour can affect productivity.

blocks.heading: Entrepreneurship: organising and bearing risk
blocks.text: Entrepreneurship organises productive resources and bears the risk of business decisions. An entrepreneur may recognise an opportunity, decide what service to offer, obtain equipment, arrange finance and combine the resources needed to operate. The venture can succeed or fail; its receipts and costs are uncertain when the commitment is made. Profit is conventionally associated with the entrepreneurial contribution, but a loss is possible. Organising a venture therefore does not imply that the owner receives a secure return. An example is a person starting a mobile bicycle-repair service who commits funds to tools and decides where to operate before knowing how many customers will buy repairs. Those tools are capital, the person's repair work is labour, and the decision to organise and risk the venture is entrepreneurship.

blocks.heading: One person can supply several contributions
blocks.text: The four-factor classification separates roles; it does not require four different people. The owner of the mobile repair business may own its tools, perform the repairs and decide how the venture is run. A salaried workshop manager can also organise daily tasks without bearing the owner's business risk. Distinguish those roles using the facts provided. Risk-taking does not mean choosing a reckless project: gathering information and planning can reduce some uncertainty, while demand and other conditions can still change. The entrepreneur compares expected returns with the resources committed and the next-best alternative use. Good coordination may improve the combination of inputs, but its results depend on the venture's circumstances. Link back to opportunity cost in topic 1.1 rather than assuming that being an entrepreneur makes the chosen activity the best use of resources.
